notes.decision: Translated 'second-instance' rather than 'Monday' or simply 'second.' Greek δευτέρα can mean both 'second day = Monday' and 'second-(instance).' In the immediate parallel structure (ⲙⲩⲥⲧⲏⲣⲓⲟⲛ // ⲇⲉⲩⲧⲉⲣⲁ), the question asks of which heavenly mystery, or of which 'second-instance' (= heavenly counterpart, cf. accumulated ⲙⲁⲍⲥⲛⲉⲩ 'second-instance' as the technical Manichaean term for earthly enactments of heavenly mysteries) Sunday is the earthly sign. The Manichaean correspondential schema strongly favors 'second-instance' over calendrical 'Monday.'

Translated 'wears upon them' though etymology is uncertain. The verb governs the Five Garments (ⲧⲧⲉ ⲛ̄ϩⲃ̄ⲥⲱ) with the First Man as subject. Most plausible analyses: (a) ⲧⲱⲱⲙⲉ 'join, touch' with 3pl object = 'has them joined to him' (i.e., wears as armor); (b) ⲧⲱϩⲙ̄ 'summon, call' with 3pl object = 'summons them' (cf. ⲧⲁⲍⲙ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ in glossary). Both fit Manichaean cosmology of the First Man's Five Sons donned as light-armor. 'Wears' captures the garment-context most directly.

Rendered literally 'the five (and) the five times' preserving the doubled pentad-structure. ⲡⲓⲧⲟⲩ = 'the five' (cf. ⲡϯⲟⲩ in glossary); the second ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲩ may be a parallel 'five' (the doublet pentad of Light, e.g. Five Sons of First Man + Five Sons of Living Spirit), or possessive 'of theirs.' ⲛ̄ⲥⲁⲡ = 'times, seasons.' Without complete context the precise structure is uncertain; the literal rendering preserves the numerical-doubling that pervades Manichaean enumerations.

Rendered tentatively 'their (own)' as a possessed feminine collective. Etymology uncertain — possibilities include: (a) Lyc plural of ⲉⲓⲱⲧ 'father' = 'their fathers'; (b) Lyc form of ⲧⲟⲩⲱⲏ 'their night' (cf. glossary); (c) ⲧⲟⲩⲏⲧⲉ as a feminine collective with ⲧⲟⲩ- prefix. Given the lacuna-laden context, no decisive reading is possible.

Obscure form (overlined) appearing twice on this page (lines 2, 4) in the construction ⲡⲧⲱⲍⲙⲉ ⲁ̄ⲃ ⲙⲛ ⲡⲥⲱⲧⲙⲉ. Possibilities: (a) abbreviated verbal form (e.g., ⲁⲃⲁⲗ 'forth' or some 'go/join' verb); (b) numerical/dual marker indicating Call+Answer as a pair; (c) Aramaic-derived ʾab 'father.' I render functionally as 'joined' to preserve the syntactic role linking Call and Answer as cooperating agents (consistent with their action in line 5: ⲭⲉⲥⲧⲟⲩ ⲁⲡⲭⲥⲉ ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲟⲧⲟⲩ 'they convey them up by their hand' — plural verb requiring both as subjects). Flag for parallel research.

Translated as 'twenty.' Lycopolitan form of Sahidic ϫⲟⲩⲱⲧ (20). Confirmed by recurrence in immediate context: ⲭⲟⲩⲧⲏ ⲛⲭⲁⲣⲁⲕⲧⲏⲣ + ⲡⲟⲩⲭⲟⲩⲧⲏ ⲙ̄ⲙⲉⲗⲟⲥ — twenty characters and twenty members of mankind, fitting the Manichaean cosmological structure of the molded human form.

Translated as 'the Father of the Living Man.' Without explicit ⲛ̄ genitive linker, the construction is ambiguous between apposition ('the Father, the Living Man') and genitive. Given the verb ⲭⲉⲥⲧϥ̄ 'conveys him up' (with 3sg.m object), the natural reading is genitive: the Father raises the Living Man (i.e., First Man / Adam). The Living Man receives the upward conveyance.

Translated as 'they were raised upward.' ⲥⲉⲍⲟ is Lycopolitan reflex of ⲥⲱϩⲉ 'stand, set up' (cf. accumulated vocabulary ⲥⲉⲍⲱ ⲁⲣⲉⲧ⸗ 'set on his feet'); with ⲁⲍⲣⲏⲓ̈ 'upward' the sense is causative-elevating, preserving vertical-soteriological semantics.

Translated as 'the Fifty.' This is the technical Manichaean term for Pentecost (πεντηκοστή = 50). The text identifies ⲡⲧⲁⲓ̈ⲟⲩ ⲡⲉ ⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲅ̄ ⲛ̄ⲍⲟⲟⲩⲉ — 'the Fifty is (consisting) of the great days,' confirming the calendar-period reference.

Translated 'seven holy days.' ⲍ̄ overlined is the numeral 7; ⲑⲟⲩⲉ (variant of ⲍⲟⲟⲩⲉ with ⲑ for ⲍ) = 'days.' These are the seven foundational holy days that the disciples of Jesus fasted from food, prefiguring the Manichaean fifty-day Pentecost.

Translated 'she filled them.' 3sg.f perfect of ⲙⲟⲩϩ 'fill' (Lyc. ⲙⲁⲍ for ⲙⲟⲩϩ). Subject is feminine ⲧⲣⲟⲫⲏ 'food' (the food of the Pentecost), filling the disciples with power, richness, life, and light.

Rendered 'they ceased being fifty days.' Standard ⲁⲩⲗⲟ ⲉⲩⲟ N construction = 'they ceased being N.' This appears to describe the typological expansion: the days extended beyond the original fifty into a hundred, perhaps reflecting the Manichaean reinterpretation of the Christian Pentecost.

Translated 'they engulfed (them)' / 'destroyed.' Lyc. reflex of Sahidic ⲧⲁⲕⲟ 'destroy, ruin' (with ⲅ for ⲕ); 3pl perfect with object suffix. Within the soteriological context of food/soul, it describes the swallowing or consuming action perhaps of dark powers within them. Confidence moderate; could alternatively be ⲧⲁⲩⲟ 'send forth.'

Read as Lyc. ⲛⲓ-ⲇⲉⲩⲧⲉⲣⲁ 'the second ones' (Greek δευτέρα). The ⲁ̄ with overline represents Greek δ following the Lyc. convention attested in ⲡⲣⲟⲁⲟⲧⲏⲥ for προδότης. Pairs antithetically with ⲛⲓϣⲁⲣⲡ̄ 'the first ones' on line 27 — first Aeons / second Aeons.

Translated 'prior' on the working hypothesis that this is a Greek-derived adjectival/verbal element from Latin/Greek 'prior'/'πρότερος' adopted into Coptic with verbalizing ⲣ̄-. The form is unusual; alternative readings include 'πρῷ-' early-stem or a corrupt form. Sense fits the kephalaion's chronological framework (events that come first in Christ's coming).
Rendered 'the coming of Jesus' per glossary entry ⲧⲟⲓⲛⲉⲓ = action-noun on ⲉⲓ 'come.'
Read as ⲛⲉⲡ-ⲛ̄ⲛ̄ⲕⲩⲣⲓⲁⲕⲏ = 'the (days) of the Sundays' — ⲛⲉⲡ- as relational/genitive cluster, with κυριακή already in glossary as 'Lord's Day'. The doubled ⲛ̄ⲛ̄ is dialectal/scribal.

Greek πεντηκοστή 'fiftieth (day) / Pentecost.' The text frames the Manichaean fifty-day Lent/fast-period as parallel to the Christian Pentecost. The apostle here gives etymological gloss: 'they call them pentecost' because of the fifty-day count.
Greek loan νηστεύω 'fast' verbalized with Coptic ⲣ̄-. Standard Coptic ecclesiastical term for ritual fasting.

Translated 'the mountain' rather than 'the four' (both attested per glossary entries ⲡⲓⲧⲁⲩ and ⲡϩⲧⲁⲩ). Context strongly favors mountain: the temptation of Christ by the devil is the standard Gospel mountain-narrative (Matt 4:8). The collocation ϩⲙ̄ ⲡⲧⲁⲩ ⲙⲡⲥⲁⲡ ⲉⲧⲁ ⲡⲇⲓⲁⲃⲟⲗⲟⲥ ⲡⲉⲓⲣⲁⲍⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁϩ = 'on the mountain at the time when the devil was tempting him' fits Matt 4 directly.
Per glossary: 'the foremost / the chief' (Lyc reflex of ϣⲟⲣⲡ̄). Likely identifying Simon as Simon Peter (the foremost of the disciples). Distinct from ⲡⲉⲧⲥⲟⲃϩ 'the leper.'
Translated 'and' as discourse-coordinator joining the new clause. Etymology unclear; possibly Lyc compound ⲁ-ϩⲁⲛ 'with-some' or coordinator. Not the same as ⲁⲍⲁⲛ 'beside' (in glossary) given context.

Untranslated lexeme of unclear identity. Tentatively 'side/edge' (possibly Lyc reflex of ⲕⲟⲩⲛ-ϩⲉ 'bosom-place' or a place-name). The full phrase ϩⲓ ⲕⲛ̄ϩⲉ ⲟⲩⲧⲱⲟⲩ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲙⲁⲩⲧ = 'at the X of a mountain of the dead' refers to a Manichaean cosmographic-narrative locus, possibly the Mount of Olives, or a primordial/eschatological Mountain of the Dead.
Lyc plural of ⲙⲟⲟⲩⲧ 'dead': 'the dead ones.' Standard Lycopolitan ⲁⲩ for ⲟⲟⲩ.
Per glossary 'upon/over' (Lyc reflex of ⲉϫⲛ̄). Here in distributive-dative sense 'I imparted (it) upon the entire Church' = bestowed upon, distributed to.

ⲙⲉⲓⲛⲉ = 'sign, type, manner' (cf. glossary ⲡⲙⲉⲓⲛⲉ 'the manner / fashion / sign'). Here in the typological correspondence: the second fifty days correspond to the type of the second Man — Christ as Second Adam in Manichaean Pauline anthropology.
